source_user: A long-context workload intermittently hits OOM after several concurrent requests. Give a prioritized diagnosis and mitigations. Scenario variant 50: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure per-request KV growth and allocator fragmentation; check max sequence and batch; inspect active sequences; test paged/prefix cache, admission control, quantization, and context limits.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions and containment: treat OOM as an unclassified resource failure until device, host, and swap telemetry identify the failing allocator. Record model revision, precision, parallelism, runtime/allocator, GPU capacity, scheduler limits, context and batch policies, and prompt/output distributions; do not infer unavailable platform facts. Reproduce in staging with a known-good configuration and cap admission while diagnosing.

Prioritized hypothesis (scenario variant 50): H1 is that concurrent live KV-cache bytes, together with allocator fragmentation, consume usable device headroom. Support H1 only if matched prompt/output-length strata show OOM probability rising with measured live KV bytes/tokens and active sequences, and failures have a smaller free margin or larger reserved-minus-allocated gap than successes. Falsify it if live KV remains bounded and fragmentation is low while a prefill workspace, activation, communication buffer, host allocation, or leak spikes. Also test max-sequence/batch overshoot, duplicated prefix-cache entries, blocks retained after completion, and runtime regressions.

Controlled experiment: replay a fixed, representative request trace with randomized paired baseline/treatment runs, warming each condition and repeating enough times to estimate uncertainty. Stratify by prompt length, generated length, concurrency, and cache-hit pattern. Change one factor at a time: first enforce a lower context/batch or concurrency limit; then compare paged KV, prefix caching, quantization, and allocator settings. Keep model, traffic, hardware, sampling, and software constant, and record every rejection. Capture request-correlated admission/prefill/decode timestamps, active sequences, per-request KV allocation/free events, KV tokens and bytes, allocator allocated/reserved/free memory and fragmentation, non-KV peaks, cache hits/evictions, GPU/host memory, and OOM stage.

Mitigation order: immediately bound maximum context, batch, and concurrency with headroom-based admission control and return explicit overload responses; ensure completed requests release KV and audit cache ownership/eviction. Next validate paged KV or prefix caching and only then consider quantization or allocator tuning, because each can change quality, latency, or fragmentation. Do not use swap or silent truncation as an unmeasured fix.

Decision and rollback: define OOM rate as OOM requests divided by admitted requests, plus rejection rate, correctness/pass rate, TTFT/TPOT, throughput, and P99. A treatment is acceptable only if it reduces OOM and preserves predeclared correctness and latency/error SLOs with uncertainty intervals; otherwise revert. Canary gradually, alert on any OOM, correctness regression, or sustained P99/rejection increase, and retain the known-good configuration. Evidence is required before attributing causality; this provisional diagnosis is not proof.
risks: platform-specific allocator or KV behavior is unknown
mitigation tradeoffs may vary by model/runtime
synthetic scenario may omit the actual OOM stage
evidence_required: request-correlated GPU and allocator telemetry
per-request live KV and active-sequence traces
repeated matched baseline/treatment replay by workload stratum
post-drain retention and fragmentation measurements
correctness, latency, throughput, rejection, and OOM denominators

Controlled experiment: replay a fixed, representative request trace with randomized paired baseline/treatment runs, warming each condition and repeating enough times to estimate uncertainty. Stratify by prompt length, generated length, concurrency, and cache-hit pattern. Change one factor at a time: first enforce a lower context/batch or concurrency limit; then compare paged KV, prefix caching, quantization, and allocator settings. Keep model, traffic, hardware, sampling, and software constant, and record every rejection. Capture request-correlated admission/prefill/decode timestamps, active sequences, per-request KV allocation/free events, KV tokens and bytes, allocator allocated/reserved/free memory and fragmentation, non-KV peaks, cache hits/evictions, GPU/host memory, and OOM stage.

Mitigation order: immediately bound maximum context, batch, and concurrency with headroom-based admission control and return explicit overload responses; ensure completed requests release KV and audit cache ownership/eviction. Next validate paged KV or prefix caching and only then consider quantization or allocator tuning, because each can change quality, latency, or fragmentation. Do not use swap or silent truncation as an unmeasured fix.

Decision and rollback: define OOM rate as OOM requests divided by admitted requests, plus rejection rate, correctness/pass rate, TTFT/TPOT, throughput, and P99. A treatment is acceptable only if it reduces OOM and preserves predeclared correctness and latency/error SLOs with uncertainty intervals; otherwise revert. Canary gradually, alert on any OOM, correctness regression, or sustained P99/rejection increase, and retain the known-good configuration.
